unit_label: Module A: Liberalised Remittance Scheme and other remittance facilities - travel foreign exchange and overseas investment

facts.statement: A resident travelling abroad may buy foreign currency notes and coins only up to USD 3,000 per visit; the balance may be carried as stored value cards, travellers cheques or bank drafts. Exceptions: travellers to Iraq and Libya may take up to USD 5,000 in notes and coins per visit; travellers to the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Russian Federation and other CIS republics may draw the entire exchange, up to USD 250,000, in notes or coins; for Haj and Umrah the entitlement of USD 250,000 may be given in cash or up to the limit set by the Haj Committee of India.

Foreign exchange for travel may be bought against rupee cash below ₹50,000; if the amount is ₹50,000 or more, the whole payment must be made by crossed cheque, banker's cheque, pay order, demand draft, debit card, credit card or prepaid card. Authorised dealers, authorised category II persons and full-fledged money changers may sell foreign exchange for travel.

On return from a foreign trip a traveller must surrender unspent foreign exchange held as notes and travellers cheques within 180 days, but may keep up to USD 2,000 in notes or travellers cheques for future use or for credit to a Resident Foreign Currency (Domestic) account; residents may hold foreign coins without limit. A resident returning from a temporary visit abroad (other than Nepal and Bhutan) may bring in Indian currency notes up to ₹25,000. A person coming into India may bring foreign exchange without limit but must declare it to customs in the Currency Declaration Form if currency notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together exceed USD 10,000 or foreign currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000 or the equivalent.

International debit cards issued by authorised dealers may be used by resident individuals for cash or merchant payments abroad within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit and only for permissible current account transactions; international credit cards from overseas issuers may be held by residents who have a foreign currency account, with charges met from that account or by remittance through a bank where the holder has an account, paid directly to the card issuer; the Reserve Bank sets no monetary ceiling on remittances under that facility; use for prohibited transactions such as lottery tickets is not permitted, and use in Nepal and Bhutan is not allowed.

Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) means acquiring unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity, subscribing as part of the memorandum of a foreign entity, investing ten per cent or more of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity, or investing with control where the holding in a listed foreign entity is below ten per cent. An investment classified as ODI continues to be ODI even if it later falls below ten per cent or the investor loses control. Financial commitment means the aggregate of ODI and debt (other than overseas portfolio investment) in the foreign entity or entities in which ODI is made, and includes non-fund-based facilities extended to or on behalf of them. A foreign entity is an entity formed outside India, including in an International Financial Services Centre, that has limited liability (except where its core activity is in a strategic sector).

The total financial commitment of an Indian entity in all foreign entities taken together must not exceed 400 per cent of its net worth as at the last audited balance sheet, or as the Reserve Bank directs with the Central Government. Capitalisation of retained earnings is not counted; utilisation of the amount raised through ADRs and GDRs, and of the proceeds of external commercial borrowings to the extent the pledge or charge on assets for them has not already been counted, is included. Financial commitment by Maharatna, Navratna or Miniratna public sector undertakings and their subsidiaries in foreign entities in strategic sectors is outside the limit. An Indian entity may make overseas portfolio investment up to 50 per cent of its net worth as at its last audited balance sheet.
facts.locator: Schedule I paragraph 3; Schedule II paragraph 1

facts.statement: No resident may make ODI in a foreign entity engaged in real estate activity (buying and selling of real estate or trading in transferable development rights, but not developing townships or constructing premises, roads or bridges for sale or lease), gambling in any form, or dealing in financial products linked to the Indian rupee without specific approval of the Reserve Bank. ODI in start-ups recognised in the host country by an Indian entity may be made only from internal accruals of the entity or its group or associate companies in India, and by a resident individual only from own funds.

payload.title: Foreign exchange for a trip: how much cash, and how to pay for it
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Cash limit**: for most destinations a traveller may buy **notes and coins only up to USD 3,000 per visit**. The rest travels as a **stored value card, travellers cheque or bank draft**.

| Destination | Notes and coins allowed |
| --- | --- |
| Most countries | **USD 3,000** per visit |
| **Iraq, Libya** | up to **USD 5,000** per visit |
| **Iran, Russia, other CIS republics** | the **whole entitlement, up to USD 250,000** |
| **Haj / Umrah** | USD 250,000 entitlement in cash, or up to the **Haj Committee's** cash limit |

**Paying the rupees**: cash is fine **below ₹50,000**. At **₹50,000 or more** the whole payment must be by **crossed cheque, banker's cheque, pay order, demand draft, or a debit, credit or prepaid card**.

**Who may sell**: authorised dealers, authorised category II persons and full-fledged money changers.

payload.title: Coming home: surrender, what you may bring in and cards abroad
payload.core_explanation_md:
**On return**
- **Surrender unspent notes and travellers cheques within 180 days**, but you may **keep up to USD 2,000** (or credit it to an **RFC (Domestic)** account).
- **Foreign coins**: hold **without limit**.
- A resident back from a temporary visit may bring in **Indian notes up to ₹25,000** (Nepal and Bhutan have their own rules).
- **Anyone arriving**: bring foreign exchange **without limit**, but **declare it to customs** on the **Currency Declaration Form** if **notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together exceed USD 10,000**, or **currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000**.

**Cards abroad**
- **International debit cards** from an authorised dealer: cash or shop payments abroad, **within the LRS limit**, **permissible current account items only**.
- **International credit cards from overseas issuers**: allowed for residents with a **foreign currency account**; pay from that account or by remittance **direct to the card issuer** through the holder's own bank. **No RBI ceiling** on this facility.
- **Never** for **prohibited items** (such as lottery tickets); **not usable in Nepal and Bhutan**.

payload.title: Overseas direct investment: what counts and what stays counted
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ODI** is an **Indian resident's investment in a foreign entity** that is any of:

1. **Unlisted equity capital** of a foreign entity.
2. **Subscription to the memorandum** of a foreign entity.
3. **10% or more** of the paid-up equity of a **listed** foreign entity.
4. **Less than 10% but with control** of a listed foreign entity.

**Once ODI, always ODI**: it stays ODI even if the holding **drops below 10%** or **control is lost**.

**Financial commitment** = ODI + **debt** (other than portfolio investment) in the foreign entity, **plus non-fund-based facilities** given to or for it.

**Foreign entity** = a body formed **outside India** (an **IFSC** counts) with **limited liability**. The limited liability condition is **waived** if its core activity is in a **strategic sector**.

payload.title: Overseas investment: the 400% ceiling and the closed activities
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Ceiling for an Indian entity**: total **financial commitment in all foreign entities together** must not exceed **400% of net worth** at the **last audited balance sheet** (or as RBI directs).

- **Not counted**: capitalisation of **retained earnings**.
- **Counted**: use of money raised through **ADRs/GDRs**; use of **ECB proceeds** (to the extent the pledge or charge on assets for them has not already been counted).
- **Outside the limit**: **Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna** PSUs and their subsidiaries in **strategic sectors**.
- **Overseas portfolio investment** by an Indian entity: up to **50% of net worth**.

**ODI is barred in**
- **real estate activity** (buying and selling property or **TDR trading**; building townships, premises, roads or bridges for **sale or lease** is not "real estate activity");
- **gambling** in any form;
- **financial products linked to the rupee**, unless the **Reserve Bank** specifically approves.

**Start-ups abroad**: an Indian entity may invest only from **internal accruals** of itself or its Indian group or associates; a resident **individual** only from **own funds**.

payload.title: How much more can the company invest overseas?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an Indian company has a net worth of ₹250 crore on its last audited balance sheet. It has already made a financial commitment of ₹680 crore in foreign entities. It now plans a further ₹400 crore of ODI. Is this within the limit, and by how much is it over or under?

worked_steps.description: The ceiling is 400% of net worth.
Compare the plan with the headroom.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The plan exceeds the 400% ceiling by ₹80 crore; the company can invest at most ₹320 crore more

self_check.prompt_text: Would raising net worth to ₹275 crore make the plan fit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ceiling becomes ₹1,100 crore, headroom ₹420 crore, which is above ₹400 crore: yes, it would fit.

payload.stem_md: A resident is travelling to Germany. What is the most foreign currency in notes and coins that he may buy for the visit?

options.explanation_md: This is for Iraq and Libya.
This is the limit for most destinations.
This is for Iran, Russia, CIS and pilgrimage.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Travellers going to countries other than the listed exceptions may buy notes and coins only up to USD 3,000 per visit.

payload.stem_md: A traveller is going to Iraq on business. How much may he take in foreign currency notes and coins?

options.explanation_md: This is for Iran, Russia and CIS.
This is the exception for Iraq and Libya.
Cash is allowed up to the limit.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Travellers to Iraq and Libya may draw foreign exchange in notes and coins not exceeding USD 5,000 per visit.

payload.stem_md: A traveller buys foreign exchange worth ₹80,000 from a money changer. How may he pay?

options.text_md: ₹49,999 in cash and the rest by cheque
options.explanation_md: The whole payment must be non-cash.
Other non-cash modes are also allowed.

options.text_md: By cheque, draft, pay order, or debit, credit or prepaid card, not by cash
options.explanation_md: At ₹50,000 and above cash payment is not allowed.

payload.correct_explanation_md: If the foreign exchange sold is worth ₹50,000 or more, the entire payment must be by crossed cheque, banker's cheque, pay order, demand draft, or debit, credit or prepaid card.

payload.stem_md: A traveller returns from abroad with unspent foreign currency notes. Within what time must he surrender them, beyond what he may keep?
payload.correct_explanation_md: On return, travellers must surrender unspent notes and travellers cheques within 180 days, but may retain up to USD 2,000.

payload.stem_md: A person arrives in India carrying foreign currency notes worth USD 6,000 and no other foreign exchange. What must he do?

options.text_md: Nothing, as the total is below USD 10,000
options.explanation_md: The USD 10,000 test concerns notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together; the notes-alone test is USD 5,000.

options.text_md: Declare them to customs on the Currency Declaration Form, because currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000
options.explanation_md: The USD 5,000 limit on notes alone is exceeded.

options.text_md: Obtain RBI approval before bringing them in
options.explanation_md: Foreign exchange may be brought in without limit.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Foreign exchange may be brought in without limit, but a declaration is needed if currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000 or notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together exceed USD 10,000.

payload.stem_md: A resident returns from a temporary visit to Singapore. How much Indian currency may he bring in?

options.explanation_md: This is the limit for temporary visits abroad.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A resident returning from a temporary visit abroad (other than Nepal and Bhutan) may bring in Government of India and RBI notes up to ₹25,000.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about international debit cards issued by an authorised dealer to a resident is correct?

options.text_md: They may be used for any purpose including lottery tickets
They have no limit at all
options.explanation_md: They fall within the LRS limit.

options.text_md: They work in Nepal and Bhutan too
options.explanation_md: Use in Nepal and Bhutan is not permitted.

options.text_md: They may be used abroad within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit and only for permissible current account transactions

payload.correct_explanation_md: International debit cards may be used for permissible current account transactions within the LRS limit.

payload.stem_md: An Indian company buys 6% of a listed foreign company and gets the right to appoint its managing director. How is the investment classified?

options.text_md: ODI, because it is an investment with control in a listed foreign entity even though below 10%
Overseas portfolio investment, because it is below 10%
Neither, as listed shares cannot be bought

options.explanation_md: Financial commitment is a measure of ODI and debt, not the classification.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Investment with control is ODI even where the holding in a listed foreign entity is below ten per cent.

payload.stem_md: An Indian company holding 12% of a listed foreign company sells down to 7% and loses control. How is the remaining holding classified?

options.text_md: Overseas portfolio investment, because it is below 10%
options.explanation_md: The Explanation keeps it as ODI.

options.text_md: Still ODI, because an investment classified as ODI continues to be treated as such
options.explanation_md: The Explanation keeps it as ODI.

options.text_md: It must be reclassified after a year

options.explanation_md: Financial commitment is a different measure.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An investment classified as ODI continues to be treated as ODI even if it falls below ten per cent or control is lost.

payload.stem_md: What is the ceiling on the total financial commitment of an Indian entity in all foreign entities together?

options.explanation_md: That is the limit on portfolio investment.

options.text_md: 400% of net worth at the last audited balance sheet

payload.correct_explanation_md: The total financial commitment must not exceed 400 per cent of net worth as on the date of the last audited balance sheet, or as directed by the Reserve Bank.

payload.stem_md: For which activity of a foreign entity is overseas direct investment by a resident NOT permitted?

options.text_md: Constructing roads for sale or lease
options.explanation_md: This is outside the definition of real estate activity.

options.text_md: Real estate activity in the sense of buying and selling property or trading in TDRs

payload.correct_explanation_md: No resident may make ODI in a foreign entity engaged in real estate activity, gambling or dealing in rupee-linked financial products without specific approval.

payload.stem_md: An Indian company wants to invest in a start-up recognised abroad. From what funds may it do so?

options.text_md: Only from internal accruals of the company or of its group or associate companies in India
From a rupee loan from a bank
From funds raised by pledging the foreign shares

payload.correct_explanation_md: ODI in start-ups by an Indian entity must be made only from internal accruals of the entity or its group or associate companies in India.

payload.stem_md: What limit applies to overseas portfolio investment by an Indian entity?

options.text_md: 50% of its net worth at the last audited balance sheet

payload.correct_explanation_md: An Indian entity may make overseas portfolio investment up to fifty per cent of its net worth as at the date of its last audited balance sheet.

payload.stem_md: An Indian company has net worth of ₹180 crore. Its existing financial commitment overseas is ₹510 crore. What is the greatest further financial commitment it can make under the 400% ceiling, in rupees crore?

A resident returns with unspent notes of USD 2,750, unspent travellers cheques of USD 1,100 and coins worth USD 40. What is the amount in dollars that he must surrender within 180 days, if he keeps the most he is allowed to?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Coins are not counted. Notes plus travellers cheques = 2,750 + 1,100 = 3,850. He may retain 2,000, so he surrenders 3,850 − 2,000 = 1,850.
